links.answerText: Queen was a multi-talented band. Brian May has a PhD in Astrophysics from Imperial College London, Freddie Mercury had a degree in Art and Graphic Design, John Deacon was an Electronic Engineer who built the Deacy Amp that Brian May uses, and Roger Taylor had a degree in Biology.
links.clue: The first song is by a band that is made up of some of the most highly educated rockstars ever, including a PhD in Astrophysics, an Electronic Engineer, a graphic designer and a biologist.
links.hint1: It is also the only band in history where every single original member has individually composed a worldwide number-one single.
links.songStartInfo: You are listening to “Another One Bites the Dust” by Queen a song that was Number 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 for Three Weeks and was the longest-running Top 10 song of 1980.
triviaItems: John Deacon was a huge fan of the disco-funk group Chic and the bass riff of Another One Bites the Dust is a direct homage to Chic’s "Good Times."
Roger Taylor famously hated this song, reportedly because of its "disco" feel, He really didn't want to use a drum loop-style beat that he thought was “un-Queen-like”.
Some Christian groups claimed that if you played the chorus backward, you could hear the phrase "It's fun to smoke marijuana."
The song remains Queen's best-selling single of all time, with over 7 million copies sold worldwide.
"Another One Bites the Dust" was the crown jewel of Queen's 1980 album, The Game, a massive turning point for the band when they shed their 70s "Prog-Rock" skin and embraced a "Pop" identity.
Freddie Mercury used to work as a baggage handler at Heathrow Airport so in 2018 the ground crew at Heathrow choreographed a "breakout" dance routine to pay tribute to their former colleague.
In 1999, the Royal Mail released a postage stamp featuring Freddie Mercury even though UK law stated that the only living people allowed to be depicted on stamps were members of the Royal Family.
John Deacon wasn't just the bassist of the band he was also an electronics engineer by training and personally built the famous Deacy Amp that is responsible for Brian May’s unique guitar sound.

links.answerText: Queen thought the song was "too disco" and didn't fit their rock image. In 1980, when Queen performed in Los Angeles, Michael Jackson went backstage and convinced them to release it. “Freddie,” he said, “you're mad if you don't release this. This is the gravy. It’s going to top the charts." It did.
links.clue: Another One Bites the Dust may never have been released as a single if it had not been for another music legend who told Freddy he was mad if he did not release it. Who was that artist?
links.hint1: Quincy Jones famously gave him the nickname "Smelly" because of his strong nose for which songs would become hits and how to market them.
links.songStartInfo: During the recording of Thriller, Quincy Jones was looking for one more "magic" ballad. Human Nature was it.
triviaItems: When "Thriller" re-entered the Billboard Hot 100 Top 10 in In November 2025 he became the first artist in history to score Top 10 hits in six different decades (the 1970s through the 2020s)
When Michael Jackson and Freddie Mercury attempted to record a series of duets in 1983 the sessions fell apart because Michael insisted on bringing his pet llama into the recording studio.
To perform the 45-degree lean in the "Smooth Criminal" video, Michael Jackson co-invented a special hitching mechanism and holds U.S. Patent No. 5,255,452 for it.
The lyrics of Human Nature were written by legendary songwriter John Bettis who wrote hits for The Carpenters. Bettis wrote the lyrics in two days.
Michael’s duet in 1995 with his sister Janet Jackson, called "Scream" holds the Guinness World Record for the most expensive music video ever made.
When Marvel Comics was facing bankruptcy, Michael Jackson seriously explored buying the company. He had met Stan Lee and desperately wanted to play Spiderman.
Michael and his brothers were part of the Jackson 5, a band that achieved something no other group in history had: their first four singles all reached Number 1 on the Billboard Hot 100.
Michael moved to New York to play the Scarecrow in the film adaptation of The Wiz. While the movie was a box-office flop, it’s where Michael met Quincy Jones who went on to become his producer.
Michael Jackson’s 1987 album Bad was the first in history to produce five Number 1 singles.
Michael Jackson’s first solo #1 song was released in 1972 and called "Ben”. It was the theme song for a horror movie about a telepathic killer rat.

links.answerText: Steve Porcaro, the keyboardist for Toto, had written a rough demo for his daughter after she came home crying because a boy at school was mean to her. He played the song for Quincy Jones and immediately knew it was the hit ballad he was looking for.
links.clue: Human Nature began life as a demo that one of the session musicians on the Thriller album had written. That musician was actually part of another killer band - name the band.
links.hint1: Collectively, the members of this band have played on over 5,000 albums, and contributed to over 225 Grammy-nominated records.
links.songStartInfo: You are listening to Rosanna by Toto, a song that is often called the "ultimate session musician's track" because it is packed with technical flourishes that most bands wouldn't dream of attempting on a pop single.
triviaItems: Writer David Paich has clarified that while he used Rosanna Arquette’s name as a placeholder, the song isn't actually about her but rather a composite of several girls he knew.
The lead dancer in the music video is a young Cynthia Rhodes who went on to star in Dirty Dancing as Penny. One of the gang members dancing in the background is a very young Patrick Swayze.
At the 1983 Grammy Awards, "Rosanna" won Record of the Year, Best Instrumental Arrangement Accompanying Vocalist, and Best Vocal Arrangement, and helped the album Toto IV win Album of the Year.
Their record label, Columbia Records, had told them that unless the album Toto IV was a massive hit, they would be dropped. This pushed them to create meticulously crafted pop-soul of this album.
The album art features a sword surrounded by four rings. The Sword was from the "Sword of Damocles" in their song "Manuela Run," and each ring represented one of their four albums to date.
This album was the last to feature original bassist David Hungate, who was replaced for the tour and subsequent albums by Mike Porcaro, the brother of Jeff and Steve.
As of today, the band is still touring under the name "The Dogz of Oz." Steve Lukather and Joseph Williams remain the core leaders, keeping the legacy alive for a new generation.

links.answerText: Steely Dan, known for sardonic lyrics and rotating casts of elite session musicians, crafted seamless masterpieces of sound—complex, polished, and intellectually sharp. They remain the gold standard for high-fidelity pop subversion.
links.clue: The drum groove on Rosanna so iconic it’s named the Rosanna shuffle. It was inspired by another song with an even more famous drum part. That band was the spiritual cousin of Toto. Name them.
links.hint1: The name of the band was borrowed from a steam-powered dildo in a William S. Burroughs novel.
links.songStartInfo: Everything You Did is a quintessential Steely Dan narrative: a cynical, jazz-inflected tale of infidelity and domestic suspicion.
triviaItems: "Everything You Did" features the tight, dry drum sound and complex chord voicings that defined Steely Dan’s mid-70s output.
Steely Dan were such perfectionists that they once spent weeks trying to record the perfect drum beat and then spliced together multiple takes into a groove that was humanly impossible to play.
Steely Dan songs often feature deeply unlikeable, unreliable, or cynical narrators, drawing more from literary fiction than typical pop songwriting tropes.
The iconic, haunting cover art of The Royal Scam was originally intended to be used for a different artist's album, but Steely Dan liked the grim cityscape so much they bought the rights.
Fagen and Becker were so obsessed with "Mu major" chords (a major triad with an added second), that this became a foundational element of the "Steely Dan sound."
The album Aja is still frequently used by audiophiles to test high-end stereo equipment due to its incredibly clean, nuanced, and layered production quality.
Legendary drummer Bernard Purdie played on many of their tracks, and famously claimed that his unique half-time shuffle was the only thing that could satisfy their rhythmic demands.
Before they were famous, Becker and Fagen had a college band called The Leather Canary. Their drummer was future Saturday Night Live star, Chevy Chase.
After 1974, Steely Dan quit touring for nearly 20 years. They preferred the controlled environment of the studio, where they could cycle through hundreds of session musicians.
Steve Gadd’s legendary drum solo on the title track of Aja was recorded in one take, despite the complex, shifting time signatures.

links.answerText: It was in reference to the Eagles that the lyric goes "Turn up the Eagles, the neighbors are listening." In response Hotel California has the line "They stab it with their steely knives, but they just can't kill the beast," as a direct reference to Steely Dan.
links.clue: Contained within Everything You Did is a playful nod to their manager, Irving Azoff and the fact that he was also the manager of another California country-rock band. Name the band. (If you listen carefully to the lyrics, you will find the answer.)
links.hint1: For a long time, this band’s Greatest Hits album was the best-selling album of the 20th century in the U.S. and is currently certified 38x Platinum.
links.songStartInfo: Love Will Keep Us Alive wasn’t released as a commercial single in the U.S. and so, wasn't eligible to chart on the Billboard Hot 100. Regardless, it became one of the most-played radio tracks of 1995.
triviaItems: The founding members (Henley, Frey, Leadon, and Meisner) actually came together as the backing band for country-rock star Linda Ronstadt before deciding to strike out on their own.
This song features the vocals of bassist Timothy B. Schmit. It became his signature song with the band, reaching #1 on the Billboard Adult Contemporary chart and staying there for eight weeks.
This song is best known from the Hell Freezes Over live MTV special. It helped define the "sophisticated soft rock" sound that allowed the Eagles to dominate the charts after their prime.
The band’s 1980 breakup was triggered by a literal onstage fight between Glenn Frey and Don Felder at a political benefit.
When they reunited for the Hell Freezes Over tour in 1994, they became the first band to charge over $100 for a face-value concert ticket. Fans grumbled, but every show sold out instantly.
The cover art for Hotel California featured the Beverly Hills Hotel, who sued. But when the shot became iconic that the hotel eventually embraced its "starring role" in rock history.
Their second album, Desperado, was a commercial flop when it was first released in 1973. Today it is considered to be a masterpiece of the "outlaw country" genre.
Founding member Bernie Leadon left the band in 1975 because he hated the shift from country to hard rock. Legend has it he punctuated his exit by pouring a beer over Glenn Frey’s head.
The Eagles were the first band to win a Grammy for Record of the Year with a rock song. Before them, the category was almost exclusively dominated by pop and jazz artists.
The band’s first big hit, "Take It Easy," was mostly written by their neighbor, Jackson Browne.

links.answerText: Traffic. The third member of The Malibu Men's Choir, the supergroup that wrote Love Will Keep Us Alive, was Jim Capaldi, the drummer of Traffic. The liner notes for the song also credit Paul Carrack (producer and co-writer of Genesis).
links.clue: As well-known as it is, Love Will Keep Us Alive, is one of the only Eagles hits not written by Don Henley or Glenn Frey. Instead, it was written as part of a side project featuring Timothy B. Schmit and Don Felder of The Eagles and the drummer of another legendary rock band. Name the band.
links.hint1: This band blended rock, jazz, and folk into progressive sound. Their most famous album features a title track about High Heeled Boys and Low Spark.
links.songStartInfo: Released in May 1967, "Paper Sun" is considered a quintessential "Summer of Love" anthem. It was a massive hit in the UK, reaching #5 on the charts, though it only peaked at #94 in the US, making it a bit of a "hidden gem" for American audiences.
triviaItems: The song is famous for its use of the sitar. Along with The Beatles' "Norwegian Wood" and "Within You Without You," it helped define the "Raga Rock" or psychedelic sound of the late 60s.
The lyrics were written by Jim Capaldi after he saw a newspaper headline about a "Paper Sun" while staying in a boarding house in Newcastle.
According to Dave Mason, the song is about a girl chasing a hollow or artificial dream. Given the era, many fans also interpreted it as a reference to the distorted reality of an LSD trip.
After recording this song, Traffic moved into a remote cottage in Berkshire, where their secluded lifestyle allowed them to write their debut album, Mr Fantasy.
Steve Winwood and Jim Capaldi were close friends with Jimi Hendrix. Winwood actually played the organ on Hendrix’s 15-minute blues epic "Voodoo Chile" from the Electric Ladyland album.
Founding member Dave Mason quit and rejoined the band three times in their first few years. He preferred pop-leaning songs, while the rest of the band wanted to play long, jazzy improvisations.
Traffic briefly broke up when Steve Winwood left to join Blind Faith with Eric Clapton and Ginger Baker. That band folded after just one album and Winwood went back to his Traffic bandmates.
The song "John Barleycorn Must Die" is an ancient English folk song that Traffic modernized to create a stoner-rock anthem.
Traffic was famous for woodwinds. Member Chris Wood often played two saxophones at the same time and incorporated flutes into their rock songs, giving them a distinct "folk-jazz" texture.
When Traffic was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2004, they were inducted by Dave Matthews, who cited them as a primary influence on the modern "Jam Band" scene.

links.answerText: In 1967, the band that would go on to be known as Status Quo wanted a more "hip" name. They called themselves Traffic Jam only to realise that Winwood’s group with a similar name was getting massive press and radio play. To avoid being seen as a "knock-off”, they quickly changed their name.
links.clue: A now-famous British band had originally called themselves Traffic Jam. When they heard Paper Sun by Steve Winwood’s new band, Traffic, they decided that discretion was the better part of valour. They changed their name and went on to become a huge success in their own right. Which band was this?
links.hint1: This band holds the all-time record for the most appearances on the UK’s Top of the Pops—over 100 times!
links.songStartInfo: Status Quo was chosen to open the Live Aid concert at Wembley Stadium. The very first notes heard by a global audience of nearly 2 billion people were the opening chords of this song - "Rockin' All Over the World." It set the high-energy tone for the rest of the day.
triviaItems: After all the trauma with their name, they looked for a name that would be classic yet "unchanging." And so they became The Status Quo in late 1967 and, in 1969, dropped “The” to become Status Quo.
To promote this song, the band filmed a music video on a barge on the River Thames. Bassist Alan Lancaster was in Australia at the time so they used a cardboard cutout of him.
In 1991, Status Quo entered the Guinness Book of World Records by performing four full arena concerts in four different cities in just 11 hours and 11 minutes.
The band is so central to British culture that they have their own brand of ale called Piledriver (named after their 1972 album) that sold over a million pints in its first nine months.
In 1982, Status Quo became the first rock band to perform a charity concert attended by a member of the British Royal Family—Prince Charles.
After being teased for decades for only using three chords, in 2007, the band released an album titled "In Search of the Fourth Chord."
In 1976, Status Quo became the first band to sign a major sponsorship deal with Levi’s. Levis credits the band for making the "double denim" (denim jacket and jeans) outfit a rock 'n' roll staple.
They have had more hit singles in the UK than any other rock band in history—more than The Beatles, The Rolling Stones, or Queen—cumulatively spending seven and a half years in the singles charts.
In 1996, Status Quo sued BBC Radio 1 for refusing to put their single "Fun, Fun, Fun" on the playlist. BBC claimed the band was "too old" for their target audience.
When King Charles III (then Prince Charles) was asked for his "desert island discs", he shocked the public by including "Down Down" by Status Quo on his list.

links.answerText: "Rockin' All Over the World" was a John Fogerty song. And of course, John Fogerty was the frontman and star of the band Creedence Clearwater Revival.
links.clue: "Rockin' All Over the World" is so widely recognised as a Status Quo song that many fans don't realise it is actually a cover. The song was originally written and recorded by the fontman of another highly regarded band as part of his 1975 solo album. Name the band
links.hint1: Before the name they are most widely known under, this band spent years recording under the name The Golliwogs.
links.songStartInfo: John Fogerty wrote "Proud Mary" the day he received his discharge papers from the Army Reserve. He was so happy to be done with military service that he sat down and wrote the riff immediately.
triviaItems: CCR holds the record for most hits to never actually reach #1 with five singles that peaked at #2 ("Proud Mary," "Bad Moon Rising," "Green River," "Travelin' Band," and "Lookin' Out My Back Door”).
CCR was almost entirely a dictatorship run by John Fogerty who wrote, arranged, produced, and sang lead on nearly every track.
Even though CCR was the first band to sign a contract for the 1969 Woodstock festival, because the Grateful Dead ran over their time, CCR didn't take the stage until 3:00 am.
The band's name was a mashup of a friend’s name (Credence Newball), words from an ad for Beer ("cool, clear water") and their commitment to "reviving" their career after their Golliwogs era.
John Fogerty was sued by his former label for plagiarising himself. The label owned the rights to the song "Run Through the Jungle" and claimed his hit "The Old Man Down the Road" sounded similar.
The band originally included John’s older brother, Tom Fogerty, who eventually quit the band in 1971 because he couldn't handle his younger brother's total control.
Most people don't realize how fast CCR moved. They released six Platinum albums in just three years (1968–1970).
One of the most famous "misheard lyrics" in rock history is in "Bad Moon Rising." While John Fogerty sings, "There's a bad moon on the rise," fans swear they hear, "There's a bathroom on the right."
"Fortunate Son" is one of the most famous protest songs of the Vietnam era, written about the unfairness of the draft and how the sons of the wealthy managed to avoid service.
When CCR was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Fogerty refused to play with his surviving bandmates but instead went on stage with a band that included Springsteen and Robbie Robertson.

links.answerText: Many people were introduced to the song “Proud Mary” when they heard Tina Turner’s version. Even though the original by CCR was just as popular in its time.
links.clue: Proud Mary was written by John Fogerty but it was made famous by another artist. So famous in fact that many people have forgotten that this was originally a CCR song. Name that artist.
links.hint1: She wrote a song about her hometown in Tennessee that is so famous in Australia, it has inspired a dance that is performed at almost every wedding.
links.songStartInfo: Private Dancer was so influential that its title was used for the 1993 Tina Turner biopic in many regions, even though the film is most famous for the title of another hit: What’s Love Got to Do with It.
triviaItems: Born Anna Mae Bullock, her husband, Ike Turner, trademarked the name "Tina Turner" so that if she ever left the band, he could simply hire another singer and call her Tina Turner.
In 2013, Tina became a Swiss citizen and relinquished her American citizenship, having lived in Switzerland since the mid-90s with her husband, Erwin Bach.
In Mad Max Beyond Thunderdome Tina Turner did her own stunts, and wore a chainmail dress weighing over 70 pounds. She also scored a massive hit with the theme song, "We Don't Need Another Hero."
Her high-energy dancing in miniskirts became her trademark. Her legs were so famous that she reportedly had them insured for $3.2 million.
Tina’s film debut was in the 1975 rock opera Tommy (by The Who), where she played the terrifying, psychedelic "Acid Queen."
In 1988, Tina broke a Guinness World Record by performing for a staggering 180,000 people at the Maracanã Stadium in Rio de Janeiro—at the time, the largest paying audience for a single performer.
When Tina finally Ike in 1976, she fled with nothing but 36 cents in her pocket and a Mobil gas credit card. She spent the next several years paying off the debts of the tour she had walked out on.
Tina credited her survival and eventual success to her Buddhist practice. She began chanting Nam Myoho Renge Kyo in the 1970s.
She wrote the song "Nutbush City Limits" about her rural hometown in Tennessee. To this day, the song is the basis for a synchronized line dance (The Nutbush) that is a cultural staple in Australia.
The theme for the 007 film GoldenEye was written for her by Bono and The Edge of U2. It remains one of the most sophisticated Bond themes in the franchise's history.

links.answerText: Mark Knopfler wrote the song "Private Dancer" for the Dire Straits album Love Over Gold, but eventually decided to scrap it. Tina’s manager who was looking for material for her comeback album, picked it up. Tina recorded it with almost the entire lineup of Dire Straits as her session musicians.
links.clue: "Private Dancer" was actually written by another band who even recorded a demo of it for their album. They ultimately decided it was written from a female perspective and "gifted" it to Tina Turner. It became the title track of her 12-million-selling album. Who was this generous band?
links.hint1: Before they were famous, this group was called The Café Racers. They changed their name to reflect how poor they were.
links.songStartInfo: Mark Knopfler wrote the lyrics of this song in an appliance store while listening to what a deliveryman was saying. Lines like "We gotta move these color TVs" and "That ain't workin', that's the way you do it" were actual quotes from the worker complaining about his job.
triviaItems: Before they became famous, the band was called The Café Racers. They changed their name to Dire Straits because they were flat broke—literally living in "dire straits."
Mark Knopfler developed this "fingerstyle" technique because the only way he could get a good sound from a poor-quality acoustic guitar was by snapping the strings with his fingers.
Brothers in Arms was the first album in history to sell one million copies on Compact Disc (CD), famously outselling its own vinyl version and helping the CD format become the global standard.
"Money for Nothing" famously mocks the excesses of MTV ("I want my MTV"), yet it became one of the most-played videos in the channel’s history and was the first video ever played on MTV Europe.
Knopfler wrote Sultans of Swing after watching a mediocre jazz band play at a nearly empty pub. At the end of their set, the singer announced, "Goodnight and thank you, we are the Sultans of Swing."
The "crunchy" guitar tone on "Money for Nothing" happened because a microphone got knocked over and ended up pointing at the floor instead of the speaker.
Mark Knopfler is naturally left-handed, but he plays guitar right-handed. This, he claims this gives him a stronger "fretting hand," allowing him to execute his bends with more precision and power.
A species of dinosaur discovered in Madagascar is named Masiakasaurus knopfleri because the paleontologists who discovered it were listening to Dire Straits at the time.
The band’s manager wanted to leave "Walk of Life" off the Brothers in Arms album entirely. Knopfler overruled him, and it went on to become one of their biggest global hits.

links.answerText: The "I want my MTV" intro is sung by Sting. He used the exact same melody as The Police’s hit "Don't Stand So Close to Me." which is why his record label sued for songwriting credit. They won, and Sting is technically a co-writer of the song, even though he only contributed one line.
links.clue: The line at the beginning of the song was sung by another famous artist who was in Montserrat while Dire Straits were recording. He dropped by the studio, sang the line, and left but his record label insisted he get songwriting credit because the melody mimics one of his own songs. Name the artist.
links.hint1: While playing with a band called the Phoenix Jazzmen, this musician frequently wore a black-and-yellow striped sweater that gave him his nickname.
links.songStartInfo: Despite being a "soundtrack song," the music industry took it very seriously as a standalone piece of art. It was nominated for Best Rock Song at the 35th Annual Grammy Awards in 1993 and lost to Eric Clapton’s "Layla" (the Unplugged version).
triviaItems: Because the movie is a "buddy cop" film, the lyrics are about a complicated, slightly cynical friendship.
One of the most unique things about the song is its percussion. If you listen to the very beginning, the clicking rhythm isn't a drum—it's the sound of a Zippo lighter being flicked open and shut.
There are two ways to hear this song— the Soundtrack Version featuring an electric guitar solo and Sting’s Version on his 1993 album Ten Summoner's Tales, a more acoustic, jazzy track.
The Police’s final (and biggest) album, Synchronicity, was inspired by the work of Carl Jung. Sting was seen reading Jung’s book on the concept of "meaningful coincidences" on the album cover.
In 1997, rapper Puff Daddy sampled "Every Breath You Take" but forgot to ask Sting for permission. Sting sued and now earns $2,000 to $5,000 a day in royalties from that song alone.
Sting is an avid chess player and once famously played an exhibition match against the world champion Garry Kasparov. Sting didn't win, but Kasparov praised his "disciplined" play.
The strange, dissonant piano chord at the beginning of "Roxanne" was a butt-chord that was recorded when Sting accidentally sat on the piano keyboard. They decided to keep it in the final track.
Sting wrote the lyrics to "Message in a Bottle" because he was fascinated by the idea of a "universal" loneliness. The music video was filmed on a small island in the Thames River.
The title of Ten Summoners Tales is a double wordplay. It’s a nod to Geoffrey Chaucer’s The Canterbury Tales, which features "The Summoner’s Tale." and a pun on Sting’s real name: Gordon Sumner.
"Fields of Gold," was inspired by the view from his 16th-century manor house, Lake House, in Wiltshire, England where he used to watch the wind blow through the barley fields outside his window.

links.answerText: Eric (Slowhand) Clapton was Sting’s collaborator on “Its Probably Me”
links.clue: It's Probably Me was composed in 1992 for the film Lethal Weapon 3. The producers wanted a theme song that combined the "cool" of 90s pop with the guitar heroics of the 70s and so they brought together Sting and one other iconic musician of the time to play on the song. Name that musician.
links.hint1: This guitarist is known by a nickname that sounds like a critique of his guitar-playing abilities, but actually refers to how the audience claps.
links.songStartInfo: "I Shot the Sheriff" is the only Eric Clapton song to ever reach number one on the US Billboard Hot 100. Despite his status as a "Guitar God," Eric Clapton has surprisingly few #1 hits. Iconic songs like "Layla," "Wonderful Tonight," and "Tears in Heaven" all peaked lower on the charts.
triviaItems: Clapton is the only person in history to be inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame three times. He was inducted with The Yardbirds (1992), Cream (1993), and as a solo artist (2000).
His most famous guitar, "Blackie," was a "Frankenstein" creation made from the best parts of three vintage Fender Stratocasters he bought in Nashville.
"Layla" was written as a desperate plea to Pattie Boyd, who was married to George Harrison at the time. The name "Layla" is from the 12th-century Persian poem, The Story of Layla and Majnun.
Clapton is the only "outsider" to play a prominent lead guitar solo on a Beatles studio track. He played the solo on "While My Guitar Gently Weeps."
In 1992, Clapton's career was revitalized by his MTV Unplugged session. The live album became the best-selling live album of all time, selling over 26 million copies.
In 1998, Clapton founded the Crossroads Centre in Antigua, a drug and alcohol treatment facility. To fund it, he has hosted several "Crossroads Guitar Festivals", raising millions for the charity.
Clapton is a world-renowned Ferrari collector. He even has a "one-off" model built specifically for him by the factory called the Ferrari SP12 EC (the "EC" stands for Eric Clapton).
In 1968, Clapton joined a "supergroup" called The Dirty Mac. The lineup included John Lennon on vocals, Keith Richards on bass, and Mitch Mitchell (of the Jimi Hendrix Experience) on drums.
He wrote Wonderful Tonight while waiting for Pattie Boyd to get ready for a party. When she kept asking, "Do I look alright?", he picked up a guitar and wrote the song out of boredom. And admiration.
Clapton was so obsessed with the blues that even when he was starting out he used to spend his last few pennies on rare American blues imports from Robert Johnson or Big Bill Broonzy.

links.answerText: Bob Marley brought reggae to the world. Even though he is a global icon of peace and spiritualism, he wrote one of the most famous "outlaw" songs in history — about an act of self-defence against a lawman. It only became a #1 hit in the U.S. after Eric Clapton covered it.
links.clue: Even though this song is widely recognised as an Eric Clapton song, it is a cover of a song by a now-famous artist who actually brought it into mainstream consciousness because Clapton "Westernised" the song. Name the artist.
links.hint1: Days after surviving an assassination attempt in 1976, this artist played a massive "Peace Concert" to unite a politically divided nation.
links.songStartInfo: "Zion Train" is one of the most spiritually and politically charged tracks from Bob Marley and The Wailers’ 1980 album, Uprising. It serves as a powerful metaphor for the soul’s journey and the Rastafarian concept of "home."
triviaItems: His birth name was Nesta Robert Marley. "Nesta" is a Jamaican word that means "messenger."
As a young child, Bob was known for his ability to read palms. At age seven, he refused to read another palm, declaring: "I am not a palm reader anymore. I am going to be a singer."
Marley was biracial (his father was a white British naval captain). Growing up in the slums of Kingston, he was often bullied and nicknamed "White Boy" by locals.
Before he became a symbol of peace, he was a formidable street fighter earning him the nickname "Tuff Gong.” He later chose this as the name for his record label and recording studio.
In 1976, gunmen broke into Bob’s home and opened fire, wounding Bob, his wife Rita, and his manager. Despite being shot, Bob performed the "Smile Jamaica" peace concert just two days later.
In 1978, during the "One Love Peace Concert," Bob achieved the impossible: he got the two warring leaders of Jamaica’s political parties to come onto the stage and clasp hands.
His greatest hits album, Legend, is the best-selling reggae album of all time having spent more than 800 weeks on the Billboard 200 chart. Since its release, it has sold 25 million copies worldwide.
Bob played soccer every single day. Ironically, it was a soccer injury to his toe that first led doctors to discover the melanoma that eventually took his life.
The inspiration for "Three Little Birds" came from three actual birds (canaries) that used to sit on the windowsill of his home at 56 Hope Road.
Bob Marley died in Miami in 1981 at the age of 36. His final words to his son Ziggy were: "Money can't buy life." He was buried in Jamaica with his red Gibson Les Paul, a Bible, and a stalk of ganja.

links.answerText: While they were never legally married, Lauryn Hill was in a long-term partnership with Rohan Marley (Bob's son), whom she refers to as her "soul's architecture." The track in question was "To Zion," from her album, The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill.
links.clue: Bob Marley's son had a son by another musician who is massively famous in her own right. Her band’s 1998 song directly referenced her husband's musical heritage. Name this famous musician.
links.hint1: Before she was famous, she was a teenage actress who co-starred with Whoopi Goldberg in Sister Act 2: Back in the Habit.
links.songStartInfo: "Killing Me Softly with His Song" was never released as a single in the United States. If you wanted to listen to the single you had to buy the full album, The Score. This was a strategy to drive album sales, and it worked—The Score went on to sell over 22 million copies worldwide.
links.songTitle: Killing Me Softly with His Song
triviaItems: Lauryn Hill was an overachiever. She was a cheerleader, a member of the track team, took violin lessons, and maintained a near-perfect GPA—all while acting in a soap opera and forming The Fugees.
The Fugees' album The Score was one of the first hip-hop albums to be certified Diamond (10 million copies) in the U.S. and is often credited with proving that hip-hop could be commercially viable.
The third member of the group, Pras Michel, was the "glue." He was the one who introduced Wyclef (his cousin) to Lauryn. Without Pras, the legendary trio would never have met.
On the song "To Zion," the acoustic guitar is played by Carlos Santana. Santana later said that working with Lauryn was one of the few times he felt he was in the presence of a "true queen."
When Lauryn won 5 Grammys in 1999 for The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill, she broke the record for the most wins by a female artist in a single night at that time.
Parts of her solo album were recorded at Abbey Road Studios because she wanted to blend "Motown" soul with "British Rock" production quality to create a sound that had no specific time or place.
Lauryn recorded the bulk of The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill at the Tuff Gong Studios in Kingston, Jamaica. This was the studio built by Bob Marley.
While auditioning for Sister Act 2, the producers were worried she was "too pretty" and "too polished" for the role. She won them over with an a cappella version of a song she wrote herself.
In 2002, she released MTV Unplugged No. 2.0. Unlike her first album, this was just Lauryn, an acoustic guitar, and raw, raspy vocals. Today, it is considered a pioneering "confessional" album.
In 2014, The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill was inducted into the National Recording Registry by the Library of Congress—the first debut album by a female rapper to receive this distinction.

links.answerText: After the song became a global hit, Roberta Flack called Lauryn Hill to thank her and told her that her version was the first time she felt the song's "soul" had been captured by a new generation. They eventually performed it together at the 1996 MTV Movie Awards.
links.clue: Today most people identify “Killing Me Softly” with Lauryn Hill and the Fugees, but it is actually much older, having first been made famous by another singer of yesteryear. Who was she?
links.hint1: A musical genius this artist was offered a full music scholarship to Howard University at 15, making her one of the youngest students ever to enroll.
links.songStartInfo: Roberta Flack made music history in 1973 and 1974 by becoming the first artist ever to win the Grammy for Record of the Year two years in a row. She won first for this song: "The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face".
links.songTitle: The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face
triviaItems: Flack is famous for her musical partnership with Donny Hathaway, with whom she recorded soul classics like Where Is the Love and The Closer I Get to You, considered the gold standard for vocal duets.

She recorded her entire debut album, First Take (1969), in just 10 hours. She was so well-rehearsed from playing in D.C. nightclubs that she sat down and knocked out nearly 40 songs in a few sessions.
For years, Roberta lived in the famous Dakota apartment building in New York City. Her next-door neighbours were John Lennon and Yoko Ono. Sean Lennon, grew up calling her Aunt Roberta.
Early in her career, when she wanted to produce her own music—a role rarely given to Black women in the 70s—she used the pseudonym Rubina Flake for her production credits to avoid industry bias.
Clint Eastwood heard her song "The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face" on his car radio while driving. He was so moved he pulled over, called her, and asked to use it in his movie Play Misty for Me.
Roberta got her start playing the organ at the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church. This early training in spiritual music gave her secular songs their trademark "holy" and hushed intensity.
Roberta is considered one of the primary architects of the "Quiet Storm" radio format—a style of smooth, sophisticated, and jazz-influenced R&B that paved the way for artists like Sade.
While recording "The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face," Roberta was mourning the death of her pet cat. She later said she channeled that specific feeling of pure, selfless love into her performance.
After she lost her ability to sing due to ALS, her contribution to music was so great that Berklee College of Music awarded her an honorary doctorate in 2023.
Her feat of winning the Grammy for Record of the Year two years in a row wasn't repeated by another solo artist for nearly 50 years until Billie Eilish did it in 2021.

links.answerText: George Michael’s cover of "The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face" is often cited by fans as one of the most intimate vocal performances of his career. George insisted on recording his vocals in the dark to help him tap into the "hushed" intimacy that Roberta Flack originally mastered.
links.clue: The song you are listening to, “The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face” was brought to the audiences of the 1990s by a British singer who has long credited Roberta Flack as one of the major influences on his vocal style. Name the artist.
links.hint1: In 1987, this artist’s "look”—leather jacket, aviator sunglasses, a single earring, and blue jeans—became an instant cultural shorthand.
links.songStartInfo: Patience was a direct message to his fans, thanking them for being "the most patient in pop history." He wrote the song during the Iraq War and he believed that "patience" was the only thing that could prevent total human destruction, a theme he explores in the lyrics.
triviaItems: George recorded much of this album at Abbey Road. He was a notorious perfectionist; it took him over four years (2000–2004) to finish the 14 tracks on the record.
George wrote the legendary saxophone riff for "Careless Whisper" while boarding a bus to go to work. He was only 17 years old at the time.
Faith became the first album by a white solo artist to reach #1 on the Billboard Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart.
During his legal battle with Sony, George refused to appear in the music video for "Freedom! '90." Instead, he hired five of the world’s most famous supermodels to lip-sync the lyrics for him.
Wham! was the first Western pop group to perform in China. The concert was a massive cultural shock with the audience sitting in stunned silence while George and Andrew Ridgeley danced on the stage.

George Michael donated all royalties from "Last Christmas" to famine relief in Ethiopia. Because the song returns to the charts every year, his estate continues to support charities with its earnings.
At the 1992 Freddie Mercury Tribute Concert, George performed "Somebody to Love" so well that rumors circulated for years that Queen had asked him to become their new permanent lead singer.
George achieved a lifelong dream when he recorded a duet with Aretha Franklin. The song, "I Knew You Were Waiting (For Me)," went to #1 worldwide and won him a Grammy.
James Corden's "Carpool Karaoke" started as a sketch with George Michael. In 2011, for Comic Relief, George and James filmed a segment where they drove around singing Wham! songs.
His 1996 album Older—which contains his version of "The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face"—was dedicated to Anselmo Feleppa, the Brazilian designer who was the "great love of his life."

links.answerText: Patience was recorded on John Lenon’s Steinway piano.
links.clue: George Michael recorded “Patience” on a Steinway piano that he bought for $2.1 million just to prevent it from leaving the United Kingdom. The piano in question belonged to one very famous rock star. Name him.
links.hint1: Instead of a traditional honeymoon, this artist and his partner invited the press into their hotel room for a "Bed-In for Peace."
links.songStartInfo: Come Together was originally written as a campaign anthem for Timothy Leary who was running for Governor of California against Ronald Reagan in 1970. His slogan was "Come together, join the party."
triviaItems: Before they were The Beatles, they were a skiffle group called The Quarrymen. John Lennon formed the band in 1956, and added Paul McCartney because he was impressed that he knew how to tune a guitar.
In 1966, John told a reporter that The Beatles were "more popular than Jesus now." This comment caused a massive firestorm in the US. "Beatle-burning" bonfires were held across the Bible Belt.
While "Yellow Submarine" is a Ringo Starr vocal, John contributed the "bubbling" sound effects in the background by blowing through a straw into a bucket of water and clinking glasses in the studio.
In 1965, all four Beatles were awarded MBE (Member of the Order of the British Empire) medals by the Queen. In 1969, John returned his in protest of Britain's support of the Vietnam War.
Fans have long believed the song Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds was code for LSD. John insisted it was inspired by a drawing his son, Julian, brought home from school of his classmate, Lucy O'Donnell.
The song Strawberry Fields Forever was named after Strawberry Field, a Salvation Army children’s home near John’s childhood home in Liverpool. He used to jump over the wall to play with the orphans.
For 46 years, "Imagine" was credited solely to John Lennon. In 2017, Yoko Ono was added a co-writer because John had admitted that much of the lyric came from her book, Grapefruit.

In 2023, the "final" Beatles song, "Now and Then," was released using a demo John recorded in New York in the late 70s. Using AI, Paul and Ringo were able to "clean" John's voice and finish the track.
The Beatles' final live performance took place on the roof of their Apple Corps headquarters in London. They played for 42 minutes before the police arrived and asked them to turn the volume down.
After a five-year "retirement" to be a stay-at-home dad to his son Sean, John returned to music with the album Double Fantasy in 1980.He was killed just three weeks after its release.

links.answerText: Chuck Berry’s publisher, Moris Levy sued for copyright infringement but instead of cash, got Lennon to agree that he would record three songs from Levy's publishing company for his next album. Lennon's 1975 album, Rock 'n' Roll, literally came into being to settle his "Come Together" debt.
links.clue: The song "Come Together" uses the line "Here come old flat-top," which was taken directly from a 1956 song by another famous musician, whose publisher promptly sued for infringement. Name the musician whose copyright had been infringed.
links.hint1: To hide the wrinkles in his rayon suit during a 1956 show, this artist crouched low and hopped across the stage on one leg while playing guitar.
links.songStartInfo: "Come On" is a bridge between 1950s Jump Blues and 1960s Rock. It features a prominent, clicking rhythm on the snare drum and a "walking" bassline. It has a clean, jazzy guitar tone that showed off his technical skill as a player, not just a showman.

links.clue: The next band were such fans of Chuck Berry, they built their early career on his catalog (including a cover of "Come On”). One day backstage, the lead guitarist picked up Chuck’s guitar and, when Chuck saw a “stranger” playing his guitar, he immediately punched him in the face. Who is this band?

links.answerText: John Lenon and Paul McCartney were the backing vocals on this song. This was evidence that there was no so-called rivalry between the two groups but just clever marketing. In return, Brian Jones (of the Stones) played the saxophone on the Beatles track "You Know My Name (Look Up the Number)."
links.clue: The high-pitched, ethereal backing vocals on “We Love You” are actually two members of a band who were allegedly the Rolling Stones’ arch rivals. It later turned out that this was one of rock’s great marketing myths—a clever "Bad Cop Good Cop” PR campaign. Name the “rival” band.

loopbackClue.clue: For the last clue, find me a connection between this song and the first song in this playlist.
correctAnswers: Billy Preston is the only musician ever to receive a joint credit on a Beatles single (for Get Back). He also played the soulful organ and piano on Another One Bites the Dust.
loopbackClue.hint1: He is often called the 5th Beatle
